title: Romania commits to 2032 coal exit to access EU recovery funds
programme: Romanian national recovery plan (coal phase-out commitment)
problem: Romania had no coal exit date while its coal regions, such as Jiu Valley and Gorj County, depended on mining and coal power.
solution: Climate conditions attached to EU recovery and Just Transition funding were used as leverage: Romania wrote a coal exit into the national recovery plan it needed to access the EU Recovery Fund. The government then mandated a commission to work out the phase-out details.
funding: EU Recovery and Resilience Facility, with Just Transition Fund support planned for Jiu Valley and Gorj County.
results: In 2021 Romania committed to exit coal by 2032; its plan cuts coal capacity by more than three quarters by 2025, which E3G says brings a 2030 exit within reach.
serbia_reason: Serbia's lignite-heavy power system will face similar EU conditions as an accession candidate, where access to funding is tied to climate commitments. Romania shows such conditions can push a coal-dependent country to set an exit date.
adapt_needed: Serbia would need to link a lignite exit date to the pre-accession and other EU funding it can actually access, not the EU Recovery Fund.
blockers: Without a comparably large EU grant envelope, Serbia has a weaker incentive to commit to an early coal exit.
quote: Climate conditionalities attached to EU recovery and Just Transition funding led to coal phase out progress in Romania. In 2021, Romania committed to phase out coal by 2032 as part of its national recovery plan developed to access the EU’s Recovery Fund.

title: Just Transition Fund ties coal-region grants to climate conditions
problem: EU transition money risked supporting regions that keep burning coal or build new fossil fuel infrastructure.
solution: The Just Transition Fund excludes nuclear and fossil fuel investments including gas, gives only 50% of annual allocations to countries not committed to 2050 climate neutrality, and requires territorial plans aligned with EU 2030 and 2050 targets and national energy and climate plans.
delivery_partners: Regional authorities preparing territorial just transition plans
funding: EU budget grants, topped up with EU recovery funding.
results: Recovery funding raised the fund from €8 billion to €19 billion, but many of the 14 territorial plans first submitted did not plan to end coal or oil shale use by 2030; the Commission said Zgorzelec County, home of the Turów mine licensed to 2044, would not be eligible.
serbia_reason: As an EU candidate, Serbia's lignite regions such as Kolubara and Kostolac will face the same rule that EU transition money excludes fossil fuels and requires plans aligned with climate targets. The Turów case shows funding can be withheld when a mine's life is extended.
adapt_needed: Serbia would need territorial transition plans for its lignite basins that are consistent with its national energy and climate plan and a coal exit timeline.
blockers: Plans to keep lignite mines operating for decades would make Serbian regions ineligible for comparable EU support.
quote: The effectiveness of these safeguards depends on the EU’s willingness to enforce their implementation. Indeed, outcomes of the WWF Territorial Just Transition Plan Assessment Tool show that many of the 14 regional transition plans submitted at that time do not plan to end coal or oil shale use by 2030 and a few even foresee investments in new fossil fuel infrastructure.

title: Transition plans in Central and Eastern Europe lack local engagement
programme: Territorial just transition plans (Just Transition Mechanism)
problem: Transition plans drafted without affected communities risk weak local ownership and low ambition.
solution: To access the Just Transition Mechanism, which aims to mobilise €55 billion in 2021–2027, member states must prepare territorial just transition plans and follow the Partnership Principle, which mandates involving trade unions, employers and NGOs.
funding: Just Transition Mechanism grants plus public and private finance for 2021–2027.
results: Analysis of plan development in Central and Eastern Europe found that targeted engagement of local people was often lacking and information flow was poor; national recovery plans also showed that weak public involvement can lead to low climate ambition.
serbia_reason: Serbia will need similar participatory transition plans for its lignite regions to meet EU funding rules after accession. The Central and Eastern European experience warns that top-down drafting undermines local buy-in.
adapt_needed: Serbia would need to fund and structure participation of municipalities, unions and civil society in transition planning for Kolubara and Kostolac.
blockers: A limited tradition of open consultation and weak local civil society capacity could restrict meaningful participation.
quote: However, analysis of transition plan development in Central and Eastern European countries shows that targeted engagement of local people is often lacking and the flow of information to them is poor, risking a lack of local ownership of the transition process.

title: EU Coal Regions in Transition initiative extended to Western Balkans
programme: Coal Regions in Transition Initiative (incl. Initiative for coal regions in transition in the Western Balkans and Ukraine)
problem: Coal regions lacked the know-how and technical capacity to prepare transition strategies and projects before dedicated EU funding existed.
solution: From 2017 the Commission ran a knowledge-sharing initiative with pilot regions, a multi-stakeholder platform and an independent secretariat delivering technical assistance. In 2020 it launched a similar initiative for the Western Balkans and Ukraine with six international partners, plus a twinning programme with EU coal regions.
delivery_partners: Six international partners (Western Balkans and Ukraine initiative)
Businesses, trade unions, NGOs and academia
results: The platform showed the need for clear rules of engagement to limit the dominance of incumbents such as the coal industry; the initiative became a workstream of the EU Just Transition Platform and was replicated for the Western Balkans and Ukraine in 2020.
serbia_reason: Serbia is covered by the Western Balkans version of this initiative, so its lignite regions can draw on EU technical support and twinning with EU coal regions. The lesson on curbing incumbent dominance applies to basins dominated by the state utility.
adapt_needed: Serbia would need to put forward pilot regions and set clear rules so municipalities and civil society, not only the utility, shape the strategies.
blockers: Technical assistance brings no investment money, and without a national coal exit date regional strategies may lack direction.
quote: The platform illustrated the importance of setting clear rules of engagement to manage the dominance of incumbents like the coal industry and clearly linking regional development discourses to climate goals. The independent secretariat of the initiative was helpful in managing this process and delivered the technical support to the regions.

title: Lusatia's generous structural aid undermined by weak regional ownership
problem: The lignite region of Lusatia had to prepare for Germany's coal phase-out.
solution: A national Structural Change Law, part of the coal phase-out, gave the region generous financial support and a governance framework; Lusatia was also an early pilot region of the EU Coal Regions in Transition initiative.
delivery_partners: EU Coal Regions in Transition initiative
funding: National funding under the Structural Change Law; the source gives no amount.
results: Regional leaders sought to delay the coal exit as much as possible and raised unrealistic expectations among workers; Germany's 2038 phase-out date was brought forward in 2021 by a new government aiming for 2030.
serbia_reason: Kolubara and Kostolac face the same risk that local leaders defend lignite and promise workers jobs that will not last. Lusatia shows that money alone does not create regional ownership.
adapt_needed: Serbia would need regional leaders to commit publicly to the exit timeline before transition funds are released.
blockers: Local political dependence on utility and mining jobs may lead Serbian regional leaders to resist or delay the transition.
quote: However, regional ownership of the transition process was hindered by regional political leadership which sought to delay phasing out coal as much as possible and created unrealistic expectations among affected workers. Germany’s 2038 phase out was brought forward in 2021 by a new government which is aiming to phase out coal by 2030.

title: Portugal closes last coal plant three years ahead of schedule
problem: Portugal needed to retire its coal plants and support affected plant workers.
solution: The government involved utilities strongly in reskilling and job creation for coal plant workers, while government and utilities invested in renewable energy and transmission grid upgrades.
results: Portugal's last coal plant went offline in 2021, three years before the phase-out date; the country targets an 80% renewables share in electricity consumption by 2030 and EDP plans 100% renewables-based electricity by 2030.
serbia_reason: Shows that pairing a coal exit with utility-led reskilling and investment in renewables and grids can allow early closure. Serbia's state utility could play a similar role for its plant workers.
adapt_needed: Serbia's plan must also cover lignite miners, since Portugal had no mines and planned only for plant workers.
blockers: Serbia's large mining workforce and high lignite dependence make its transition far bigger than Portugal's.
quote: Its last coal plant went offline in 2021, three years before the country’s phase out date. Transition planning focuses on coal plant workers as Portugal has no mines.

title: Late coal exit dates in national climate plans destabilise transitions
programme: National Energy and Climate Plans (Poland, Czechia, Bulgaria)
problem: Without a clear EU signal that coal must end by 2030, some governments planned coal use well beyond that date.
solution: Poland, Czechia and Bulgaria set late coal retirement timelines in their mandatory National Energy and Climate Plans.
implementer: Governments of Poland, Czechia and Bulgaria
results: Based on their plans, the three countries would produce over 95% of the EU's planned coal electricity in 2030; E3G warns this forces frequent later adjustments and reduces planning security for regions and workers.
serbia_reason: Serbia must also prepare a national energy and climate plan under its Energy Community obligations, and the lignite timeline in it will shape regional planning. An unrealistically late date risks the same disruptive corrections later.
adapt_needed: Serbia's plan would need a lignite retirement path consistent with EU 2030 and 2050 targets.
blockers: Heavy reliance on state-owned lignite power and security-of-supply concerns push towards late retirement dates.
quote: Settling for a late coal phase out date creates an unstable transition process and will make more frequent adjustments necessary as politics and market conditions in the EU make a 2030 phase out unavoidable. This decreases planning security for affected regions and exposes workers and industry to disruptive changes.

title: Horná Nitra's locally led transition plan wins national approval
programme: Horná Nitra (Upper Nitra) transformation action plan
problem: The Slovak lignite region Horná Nitra needed a transition plan before any dedicated EU transition fund existed.
solution: Local authorities started a transition plan in 2018 with strong community engagement, supported by the EU Coal Regions in Transition Initiative.
delivery_partners: EU Coal Regions in Transition Initiative
results: The national government approved the action plan in 2019, and Slovakia committed to a coal phase-out by 2023 and joined the Powering Past Coal Alliance in 2019.
serbia_reason: Shows that municipalities in a lignite region can start transition planning themselves and win national backing. Serbian mining municipalities could do the same ahead of a national exit decision.
adapt_needed: Serbian municipalities would need technical support and a formal mandate to plan, since energy policy is decided centrally.
blockers: Without a national coal exit date, the government may not endorse a local transition plan.
quote: The plan was approved by the national government in 2019 and supported by the EU’s Coal Regions in Transition Initiative.
